question: Why does training a deep network inside a random affine subspace exhibit a threshold number of trainable degrees of freedom, how should that threshold depend on target loss and initialization, and how does it compare with pruning-informed subspaces?

key_findings.claim: Restricted training exhibits an empirical phase transition: at a fixed target loss, the observed success probability moves sharply from near zero to near one as random-subspace dimension increases, and the transition shifts to lower dimension after more burn-in training.
key_findings.evidence: The authors sweep affine-subspace dimension for Conv-2, Conv-3, and ResNet-20 across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and related small vision datasets. Figures 2, 3, 7, and 8 show the phase boundary for random initializations and several burn-in times. The operational success event is the best loss reached by Adam, which the paper correctly describes as only a lower-bound proxy for geometric intersection.

key_findings.claim: Gordon's escape theorem relates the threshold to the angular size of the target loss set around the initialization: a random affine subspace is likely to miss when its dimension plus the squared Gaussian width of the spherical projection is below the ambient parameter dimension.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines local angular dimension as w(proj_w(S)) squared and derives the high-probability miss condition from Gordon's theorem. This makes target loss and initialization geometrically explicit: larger sublevel sets or an initialization closer to them generally subtend a larger angle and require fewer random directions.

key_findings.claim: The displayed equality d*=D-d_local is stronger than the theorem proved for an arbitrary neural-network loss set.
key_findings.evidence: The paper's stated Gordon bound supplies a high-probability escape direction. It notes that matching intersection bounds require spherical convexity and otherwise may guarantee intersection only with a spherical convex hull. In addition, optimization success is not the same event as nonempty intersection. Thus equation 3.3 is a useful phase-boundary model, but not a general exact theorem for nonconvex loss sets optimized by Adam.

key_findings.claim: For a quadratic well, the framework predicts how Hessian anisotropy and distance to the optimum change the threshold, and simulations follow the resulting upper-bound trend.
key_findings.evidence: An ellipsoidal loss sublevel set has axes proportional to sqrt(epsilon/lambda_i). The paper lower-bounds its projected angular dimension by a sum of r_i squared over R squared plus r_i squared, yielding an upper bound on the needed training dimension; Figure 5 compares that approximation with two synthetic Hessian spectra and three initialization distances.

key_findings.claim: Trajectory-informed lottery subspaces reach the reported full-model accuracy in only about 20-60 retained directions, but this is an ex-post diagnostic rather than a cheap pruning algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: Lottery subspaces are the leading principal components of an already completed full-space training trajectory. Figures 3 and 6 show them outperforming random affine subspaces and lottery tickets at high compression. The appendix also reports optimization failures after adding low-singular-value directions, which the main plots hide with a running maximum.

method.core_idea: Treat restricted neural-network training as a random affine-subspace intersection problem and use Gaussian width to quantify how much of the surrounding sphere is occupied by a desired loss sublevel set.
method.mechanism: Train from a random or partially trained offset in Gaussian random subspaces of increasing dimension; estimate a success-probability phase boundary; project the target loss set onto the unit sphere around the offset; apply Gordon's escape theorem; and compare with axis-aligned lottery tickets and PCA subspaces extracted from a full training trajectory.
assumptions: Random Gaussian directions, after normalization, represent uniformly random subspaces.
The target sublevel set is closed; sharp two-sided intersection claims require additional spherical-convexity or convex-hull qualifications.
Adam's best attained loss is an adequate empirical proxy for whether the chosen subspace intersects the target set.
Small vision networks and short training runs expose geometry representative enough to motivate broader claims.

techniques.role: Operationalizes the phase boundary in restricted-training success.
Measures a loss set's squared Gaussian width after projection around an initialization.
Provides the high-dimensional random-subspace miss condition.
Separates the effect of initialization quality from random direction count.
Builds an optimized general subspace from a completed training trajectory.

evaluations.setting: Conv-2, Conv-3, and ResNet-20 on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, with additional CIFAR-100 and SVHN runs
evaluations.metric: Probability of reaching train/test accuracy thresholds versus trainable subspace dimension
evaluations.result: Sharp empirical boundaries appear, and longer burn-in generally lowers the dimension required for high accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: Full-space training and random affine subspaces from initialization

evaluations.setting: Synthetic quadratic wells with bimodal and continuous Hessian spectra
evaluations.metric: Measured threshold dimension versus the analytic upper bound
evaluations.result: Simulated phase boundaries track the predicted dependence on target loss, Hessian spectrum, and distance from the minimum, with a looser bound closer to the well.

evaluations.setting: Compression comparison on small vision networks
evaluations.metric: Accuracy versus full-parameter-count divided by restricted training dimension
evaluations.result: Lottery subspaces are strongest in the overlapping high-compression region; lottery tickets usually do not beat random affine subspaces there, with a Conv-2/CIFAR-10 exception.
evaluations.baseline: Random affine, burn-in affine, magnitude-pruned lottery tickets, and the full model

evaluations.metric: Threshold dimension of the nonlinear network versus an NTK linearization around one optimum
evaluations.result: The reported threshold curves are similar in these two cases, offered as evidence that a basin-local linearization may be useful.

limitations: The experiments use small image models, short runs, and no transformer- or foundation-model-scale validation.
Only 10, 5, or 3 runs per point are used depending on architecture, and delta is changed accordingly.
The geometry proves an intersection/escape statement, whereas the experiment measures optimizer success; the gap can be material in nonconvex landscapes.
The sharp converse needs spherical convexity or concerns a convex hull, so exact equation-3.3 language should not be read as unconditional.
Lottery subspaces consume a complete full-space trajectory and expensive projection machinery before reporting their small retained dimension.
The random-subspace comparison reaches at most dimension 4096, limiting overlap with less compressed lottery tickets.
failure_modes: A subspace can intersect a low-loss component that Adam fails to find, inflating the empirical threshold relative to the geometric one.
Nonconvex disconnected sublevel sets can violate the intuition that Gaussian width alone supplies an exact transition.
Burn-in can provide no benefit, as observed for Conv-3 on MNIST, or can merely start near the requested accuracy rather than reveal better directions.
Low-singular-value trajectory directions can make lottery-subspace optimization worse even though the nested subspace still contains earlier solutions.
Global magnitude pruning can collapse an entire layer at high compression.
reusable_insights: Report restricted-training success as a probability curve, not a single intrinsic-dimension number.
Condition degrees-of-freedom claims jointly on target performance and initialization quality.
Distinguish geometric existence, optimizer reachability, and total cost of discovering a subspace.
Use trajectory spectra as a diagnostic upper target for practical compression, while charging the full trajectory used to obtain them.
open_questions: Can local angular dimension be estimated without thousands of restricted retraining runs?
What two-sided intersection guarantees apply to realistic disconnected neural loss sublevel sets?
Do burn-in and Gaussian-width predictions persist for transformers and modern pretraining objectives?
Can a useful lottery subspace be identified online without first storing and decomposing a complete full-space trajectory?
How much of the observed phase transition comes from landscape geometry versus the optimizer's own dimension-dependent conditioning?

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. introduced the empirical dimension at which solutions appear across supervised and reinforcement-learning tasks; this paper replaces a single performance threshold with loss/initialization-dependent phase curves and a Gaussian-width explanation.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Neural Network Training in Low Dimensional Random Bases
competitive_landscape.difference: Gressmann et al. redraw and factor random projections to improve optimization and memory; this paper keeps subspaces fixed to study the geometry of the success threshold and initialization.

competitive_landscape.title: Intrinsic Dimensionality Explains the Effectiveness of Language Model Fine-Tuning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Random-subspace analysis of pretrained language models
competitive_landscape.difference: Aghajanyan et al. measure low-dimensional fine-tuning and connect it to generalization; this paper studies training loss-sublevel geometry, burn-in, and phase transitions on smaller vision networks.

competitive_landscape.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Lottery tickets select coordinate-aligned subnetworks by iterative magnitude pruning; the present work places them in a taxonomy with general affine subspaces and introduces trajectory-PCA lottery subspaces.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper gives a high-dimensional geometric explanation for threshold training dimension, introduces local angular dimension, and proposes burn-in and lottery subspaces for comparing restricted-training methods.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The Gordon-width formulation explicitly predicts the effects of target loss and initialization, is illustrated on quadratic wells, and is paired with phase maps across several small vision settings.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The initialization-conditioned geometric reframing is the durable contribution. Its exact-threshold wording and compression implications require the convexity, optimizer, scale, and full-trajectory cost caveats retained above.

reviewer_notes: Read all 20 extracted pages, including the complete empirical supplement, raw lottery-subspace spectra, NTK comparison, hyperparameters, and theory supplement. The competitor panel was checked against primary arXiv/OpenReview records on 2026-08-23.
